To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

when a stimulus is associated with an outcome that is the same as the outcome associated with that stimulus on a preceding trial, the stimulus is learned more quickly than when the stimulus is associated with a different outcome.

when the same stimulus element has the same status as in the preceding reversal, learning is faster, but when both stimulus elements have the opposite status as in the previous reversal, learning is slower.

the rate at which rats learned a discrimination reversal involving two-link chains was influenced by the status of the chain elements on the preceding reversal, with learning being faster when both elements had the same value as on the preceding trial and being slower when both had the opposite value as on the previous trial.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how animals learn the value of stimuli that have no inherent value.
the nature of the information that is transmitted in learning involving stimulus chains.
the question of whether or not the stimulus elements that constitute a stimulus chain acquire value in a manner analogous to that by which a single stimulus acquires value.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data are consistent with a theory in which stimulus value is transmitted backward along a stimulus chain.
the data support the hypothesis that backward chaining of stimulus values is a major mechanism in the transmission of value in discrimination learning involving chains of stimuli.
the data support an interpretation in terms, at least in part, of the backward chaining of value.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
stimulus value is transmitted backward in a stimulus chain.

the rate at which a stimulus is acquired as a signal for a particular event is proportional to the rate at which the event occurs in the presence of that stimulus, regardless of whether the stimulus is presented before or after the occurrence of the event.
backward chaining is the most important mechanism for value transmission in discrimination learning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the backward chaining model can account for the data from a wide range of experiments involving stimulus chains.

the backward chaining of stimulus elements in the discrimination learning of rats is a robust phenomenon that is not dependent upon the presence of a single stimulus element that is consistently associated with one outcome.
stimulus chains can be used in a variety of ways to enhance or disrupt discrimination learning.
